questions.prompt: What is the goal of a spring if it is extended or squeezed, and what does a mass that is already moving do? Why do these two facts together make the system vibrate?
questions.answer: A spring wants to go back to equilibrium, its resting length, so it pulls or pushes the mass back there. A mass that is already moving keeps on moving. When the spring brings the mass back to equilibrium, the mass is still moving, so it overshoots and squeezes or stretches the spring on the other side, and the spring sends it back again, so the system goes back and forth.
rubric: Overshoot past equilibrium repeats the cycle.

questions.prompt: If I raise the mass of a mass-spring system, does the frequency rise or fall? And if I raise the stiffness? Explain why for each.
questions.answer: Raising the mass makes the frequency fall, because a heavier mass is harder to get moving and harder to turn around, so each trip back and forth takes longer. Raising the stiffness makes the frequency rise, because a stiffer spring pulls back harder and turns the mass around sooner.

questions.prompt: A mass between two walls is pulled up and let go, so it moves up and down instead of along the spring. Why does it still vibrate like a mass on a spring?
questions.answer: Pulling the mass up stretches the springs, and springs hate being stretched, so they pull it back down. When the mass passes the middle the springs are not stretched, but the mass is moving, so it keeps going and stretches them on the other side. That is the same stretch and release as the longitudinal system, so it vibrates the same way.
rubric: Springs stretch when the mass moves up.
The moving mass overshoots the middle.

questions.prompt: Why does a two-mass system have two frequencies, and why is Mode 2 faster than Mode 1?
questions.answer: Two masses can move together or against each other, so they have two modes. In Mode 1 they move together, and the middle spring rides along without stretching, so only two springs are really working. In Mode 2 they move against each other and all three springs stretch and compress, so more stiffness is working and Mode 2 vibrates faster.
rubric: More springs working means higher frequency.

questions.prompt: How many modes does a 4-mass system have, and which one has the highest frequency? Why?
questions.answer: A 4-mass system has four modes, because N masses give N modes. Mode 4 has the highest frequency, because in Mode 4 every mass goes against its neighbors, so every spring stretches and compresses the most and the system goes back to equilibrium fastest.
rubric: Every spring working gives the most stiffness.

questions.prompt: In a two-mass system, if you make the spring between the two masses stiffer, what happens to Mode 1 and Mode 2, and why?
questions.answer: Mode 1 stays the same, because in Mode 1 the masses move together and the middle spring never stretches, so its stiffness does not matter. Mode 2 goes up, because in Mode 2 the masses move against each other, the middle spring is stretched and squished, and a stiffer spring pulls back harder.
rubric: A spring matters only where it stretches.

questions.prompt: A string is fixed at both ends and Mode 1 is 150 Hz. What are the frequencies of Modes 2, 3 and 4, and why are they spaced this way?
questions.answer: Mode 2 is 300 Hz, Mode 3 is 450 Hz and Mode 4 is 600 Hz. Both ends must stay still, so each higher mode fits a whole number of copies of the first half wave into the string, and each extra copy adds one more base frequency.
rubric: Counting copies of the first mode.

questions.prompt: Describe the theory, the prediction and the experiment for the vocal folds as a vibrating system.
questions.answer: The theory is that the vocal folds are a membrane of masses and springs fixed on its edges. That theory predicts that the voice will have a spectrum with evenly spaced spikes, the harmonics, at multiples of the base frequency. The experiment took a spectral slice of a voice in Praat, and the second spike came out at about double the first and the third at about triple, so the prediction held.

questions.prompt: What is different about a system that is fixed at one end and free at the other, compared with one fixed at both ends?
questions.answer: A fixed-free system has no motion at the fixed end and the most motion at the free end, so its basic piece runs only from still to moving. Its modes fit only odd numbers of those pieces, so its frequencies are odd multiples of the first, while a system fixed at both ends has every whole-number multiple.
rubric: Still at fixed end, most motion at free end.

options.feedback: Stiffness pulls back harder, which speeds the vibration up.

options.feedback: Both mass and stiffness set the frequency.

options.text: It rises only if the mass is also raised.
options.feedback: Raising mass would push the frequency the other way.

questions.answer: Correct. Stiffness up means frequency up.
rubric: The best answer is It rises, because a stiffer spring pulls the mass back faster..

questions.prompt: Why do multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies?
questions.answer: Several masses can vibrate in several modes, because they can move together or against each other. The more the masses go against each other, the more the springs stretch and compress, so more stiffness is working and the mode is faster. So each mode has its own frequency, and N masses give N frequencies.
rubric: More springs working in higher modes.

questions.prompt: In a three-mass system, if you make the middle mass heavier, what happens to the frequency of each mode, and why?
questions.answer: Mode 1 goes down, because the middle mass moves in Mode 1. Mode 2 stays the same, because the middle mass is frozen in Mode 2, and a mass that does not move has no effect. Mode 3 goes down the most, because the middle mass moves the most in Mode 3, and the more a mass moves, the more its weight lowers the frequency.
rubric: Mode 2 unchanged because the mass is still.

questions.prompt: What do you get when you have an infinite number of masses and springs, and why does it still have modes?
questions.answer: You get a string. Every little piece of a string has mass and every little piece stretches like a spring, so the string can vibrate in modes just like a chain of masses, with more and more bumps in the higher modes.
rubric: Each piece has mass and springiness.

questions.prompt: A small section of a string moves a lot in Mode 4 but does not move at all in Mode 5. If we raise both the mass and the stiffness of that section, what happens to Mode 4 and Mode 5, and why?
questions.answer: Mode 4 goes down, because the section is moving in Mode 4, so the added mass lowers the frequency, and the added stiffness does nothing since the string there is not stretching. Mode 5 goes up, because the section is still in Mode 5 but stretching a lot, so the added stiffness raises the frequency, and the added mass does nothing since it is not moving.

questions.prompt: What is perturbation, and what happened when wax was added to different parts of a drum?
questions.answer: Perturbation is changing one small part of a vibrating system and predicting how each mode responds. When wax, which adds mass, was put where the drum vibrated the most, the frequency dropped. When it was put where there was no motion, the frequency did not change, because a mass that does not move has no effect.
rubric: Wax at a moving spot lowers frequency.
Wax at a still spot does nothing.

questions.prompt: Why can heavy smoking change how a voice sounds, in terms of masses and springs?
questions.answer: Smoking can create nodules on the vocal folds, which add a little mass to one spot, and it changes the stiffness and mass of different parts of the folds. Those local changes shift different modes by different amounts, just like wax on a drum, so some harmonics stop being perfect multiples of the base frequency and the voice sounds different.

questions.prompt: Why is a building a fixed-free system, and why do engineers design it to sway only in Mode 1?
questions.answer: A building is fixed to the ground at the bottom and free to sway at the top, so it is fixed at one end and free at the other. In Mode 1 the whole building sways together, which is safe. In higher modes, some floors would move one way while others moved the other way, which would shatter the structure.
rubric: Fixed at the ground, free at the top.
Higher modes put floors against each other.

questions.prompt: Why does adding mass at the very edge of a string fixed at both ends do nothing to its frequency, while adding mass in the middle of Mode 1 lowers it a lot?
questions.answer: The edges of the string are fixed, so they never move, and a mass only affects frequency in proportion to how much it moves. In the middle of Mode 1 the string moves the most, so extra mass there is very hard to turn around and lowers the frequency a lot.
rubric: Middle of Mode 1 moves the most.

questions.prompt: For the vowel /u/, why do both F1 and F2 go down when the lips are rounded?
questions.answer: Rounding the lips squeezes the air at the free end of the tube, which raises its mass and its stiffness. At the free end the air moves back and forth a lot in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, with hardly any compression. So the added mass lowers both formants, and the added stiffness does nothing.
rubric: Air there moves in both modes.
Added mass lowers F1 and F2.

options.feedback: The middle moves in odd modes, so it is not always springy.

questions.answer: Correct. Maximal stretching goes with no movement.
rubric: The best answer is At the points that do not move, including the fixed ends.

questions.prompt: If something raises both the mass and the stiffness of a system, why don’t the two effects simply cancel out in a system with many masses?
questions.topic: Mass and stiffness do not cancel
questions.answer: In a system with many masses, the places with the most motion are the places with the least springiness. At a spot that is still but stretching, only the added stiffness counts, so the frequency goes up. At a spot that moves but does not stretch, only the added mass counts, so the frequency goes down. So which effect wins depends on where the change is.

questions.prompt: Why are the formants of a fixed-free system 1, 3, 5 and so on multiples of the base frequency?
questions.answer: The basic piece of a fixed-free system is a quarter-wave packet that runs from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end. Every mode must start still at the fixed end and end moving at the free end, so adding one packet would leave a still point at the free end. Packets get added two at a time, which gives one, three, five and seven packets, so the formants are odd multiples.
rubric: Quarter-wave packet from still to moving.
Ends must stay still and moving.
Packets added two at a time.

questions.prompt: A system is fixed at one end and free at the other, and its first formant is 500 Hz. What are its next two formants, and why not 1000 Hz?
questions.answer: The next two formants are 1500 Hz and 2500 Hz, three and five times the first. A fixed-free system only has odd multiples, because each mode has to fit an odd number of quarter-wave packets, so a mode at two times the base cannot exist.

questions.prompt: What is a formant, and what part of speech has formants?
questions.answer: A formant is a frequency of vibration of a system that is fixed on one side and completely free on the other. In speech, the air in the vocal tract is that system, fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the lips, so its formants are what make the vowels and consonants.
rubric: Fixed at the folds, free at the lips.

questions.prompt: In the air of the vocal tract, how can you tell where the air acts like a mass and where it acts like a spring? Where is each one always found?
questions.answer: Where neighboring bits of air come close together and then spread apart, the air is compressing and expanding, so it is acting like a spring. Where the air just moves back and forth together without its spacing changing, it is acting like a mass. The air near the closed vocal folds is always springy, and the air at the open lips always acts like a mass.
rubric: Springy at the folds, mass at the lips.

questions.prompt: Why does constricting the vocal tract raise both the mass and the stiffness of the air there?
questions.answer: Squeezing air makes it stiffer, the same way pumping up a tire makes it stiffer. Squeezing air into a smaller space also raises its density, so the constricted air is effectively heavier. So a constriction always adds both stiffness and mass at that spot.

questions.prompt: For the vowel /i/, the constriction is two thirds of the way up from the vocal folds. Why does F1 go down while F2 goes up?
questions.answer: At that spot the air in Mode 1 is mostly moving back and forth, so it acts like a mass, and the added mass lowers F1. In Mode 2 the air at that same spot is mostly compressing, so it acts like a spring, and the added stiffness raises F2.
rubric: Mode 1 moving there, so F1 down.
Mode 2 compressing there, so F2 up.

questions.prompt: For the vowel /a/, the constriction is about one third of the way up from the vocal folds. Why does F1 go up while F2 goes down?
questions.answer: In Mode 1 that spot is close to the closed end, where the air is always springy, so the added stiffness raises F1. In Mode 2 that same spot falls where the air is moving like a mass between two compressed regions, so the added mass lowers F2. So /a/ is the opposite of /i/.
rubric: Mode 1 springy near the closed end.

questions.prompt: What is the source and what is the filter in a vowel, and how do they work together?
questions.answer: The source is the vocal folds, which supply the harmonics at multiples of F0. The filter is the shape of the vocal tract, whose formants decide which harmonics come through. Harmonics close to a formant are made louder, and harmonics far from any formant are muted, so the formants do not make new frequencies but choose which of the source’s harmonics are heard.
rubric: Vocal tract shape is the filter.

questions.answer: Correct. The tract is fixed at one end and free at the other.
rubric: The best answer is They are odd multiples of the first formant.

questions.prompt: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and the formant rises a great deal, what must be true of air motion versus springiness at that spot?
questions.answer: At that spot the air must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode. A constriction raises both mass and stiffness, and the formant only rises when the added stiffness counts, which happens where the air compresses and expands. The added mass did nothing, because the air there was not moving.
rubric: Mass has no effect without motion.

questions.prompt: Describe a spectrogram.
questions.answer: A spectrogram stacks many spectra side by side over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis and frequency runs up the vertical axis, and the darker a spot is, the more amplitude there is at that frequency and time. The formants show up as dark bands, so you can watch them rise and fall as the speaker changes sounds.
rubric: Formants as dark bands that move.

questions.prompt: If the vocal folds have F0 at 120 Hz, what are the first four harmonics? What happens to their spacing if the folds become tighter and lighter?
questions.answer: The first four harmonics are 120, 240, 360 and 480 Hz, because the vocal folds are fixed on their edges and give whole-number multiples. If the folds become tighter and lighter, F0 goes up, so the harmonics are spaced farther apart.

questions.prompt: Why are opera singers and very small children hard to understand, in terms of source and filter?
questions.answer: Both have a very high F0, so their harmonics are spaced far apart. A formant can only make the harmonics near it audible, so when the harmonics are sparse, some formants have no harmonic close by to amplify. The listener then cannot hear where the formants are, so it is hard to tell which vowel is being said.

questions.prompt: What is the core rule for how formants interact with harmonics?
questions.answer: A formant encourages the harmonics closest to it to be audible, and harmonics far from that formant are muted. So the formants do not create new frequencies, they decide which harmonics of the voice come through strongly.

questions.prompt: An m was cut from "ma" and pasted in front of the vowel from "na." What did listeners hear, and what does that mean about speech perception?
questions.answer: Listeners heard "na," even though the consonant came from "ma." The vowel after n has a formant that drops sharply, and listeners used that drop to decide the consonant. So people do not decide sound by sound, they take in a stretch of speech and decide about a consonant later, during the vowel, and a machine that understands speech has to do the same.

questions.prompt: What in speech is a building analogous to, and why does the analogy hold?
questions.answer: A building is analogous to the air in the vocal tract. Both are fixed at one end and free at the other, the building at the ground and the air at the closed vocal folds. So both have the same kind of modes, with springiness at the fixed end, the most motion at the free end, and frequencies at odd multiples.

questions.prompt: Where is the knowledge of a neural network stored, and why does a network with random weights make a bad decision?
questions.answer: The knowledge is stored in the weights, the positive and negative numbers on the connections. A positive weight pushes the next neuron up and a negative one pushes it down. Before training the weights are random, so they push the activations in meaningless directions, and the decision at the end is basically a guess.

questions.prompt: How many hidden layers does this network have? net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.Linear(4, 3), nn.Linear(3, 5))
questions.answer: It has two hidden layers, with four neurons and three neurons. The network takes in two numbers, passes them through those two hidden layers, and the last line makes the five outputs, so the second number of every line except the last is a hidden layer.
rubric: Last line is the output layer.
Input layer has no line of its own.

questions.prompt: Describe in your own words how forward propagation gets from the input to a decision.
questions.answer: The input numbers, such as F1 and F2, go into the first layer. Each neuron multiplies every incoming number by its weight and adds the results, which is an inner product, and that sum becomes its activation. Those activations are the inputs to the next layer, which does the same thing, layer by layer, until the last numbers are turned into a probability distribution and the category with the highest probability is the decision.
rubric: Probabilities and the highest one is the decision.

questions.prompt: A hidden neuron with a positive activation connects to the output "done" with a positive weight. If that activation goes up, what happens to the probability of "done," and why?
questions.answer: The probability of "done" goes up. The contribution of that neuron is its activation multiplied by its weight, and both are positive, so making the activation bigger makes the contribution bigger. That raises the score for "done," so its probability rises, and since the probabilities add up to one, the others go down a little.

questions.prompt: Why does backpropagation change the last weights first and work backward to the first weights?
questions.topic: Why backpropagation starts at the end
questions.answer: The last weights are the easiest problem, because they feed straight into the output, so changing them changes the probabilities directly. The first weights are the hardest, because their effect is buried under every later layer of activations and weights. Like dynamic programming, it solves the easiest problem first, and solving the end first makes the next layer back easier, all the way to the start.
rubric: Last weights directly change the decision.
First weights act through many layers.

questions.prompt: The network’s decision is [.2, .1, .5, .1, .1], but the true category is the one in the first position. Using Python list notation, how do we tell the network the right answer, and what does it do with it?
questions.answer: The desired output is [1, 0, 0, 0, 0], with all of the probability on the true category. The network compares its own output with this desired output to get its error, and backpropagation uses that error to change the weights so the true category gets a higher probability next time.

questions.prompt: Is [.3, .3, .2, .3] a valid decision of a neural network with four categories? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. A probability distribution needs every number between zero and one and all of them adding up to one, and these add up to 1.1, which is more than one.

questions.prompt: What does the sigmoid do to a neuron, and where did the idea come from?
questions.answer: The sigmoid takes a neuron’s inner product and turns it into a number between zero and one, so the neuron becomes nearly digital, either mostly off or mostly on. The idea comes from Adrian’s discovery that real neurons are nearly digital, because they either fire or do not fire. So neural networks did not come out of nowhere, they copy what was found in animal brains.

questions.prompt: What do the lines "import torch" and "from torch import nn" do, and what does nn.Sequential mean?
questions.answer: The import lines bring into Python a library with everything needed for inner products, backpropagation and related work, so none of it has to be written by hand. nn.Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers, one after another, which describes every network built so far.
rubric: Inner products and backpropagation come with it.
Sequential means a sequence of layers.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard to know which way to change a weight in the first layer?
questions.answer: Changing a first-layer weight changes that layer’s activations, which change the next layer’s activations, which change the layer after that, and only then the probabilities. Its effect is mixed with many other weights along the way, so looking at the weight alone says little about what it will do to the decision.

questions.prompt: How is backpropagation like dynamic programming?
questions.answer: Dynamic programming solves the smallest, easiest problems first and uses their answers to solve the bigger problems that contain them. Backpropagation does the same by fixing the last weights first, then using what it learned to fix the layer before, all the way back. Combined with stochastic gradient descent, which changes each weight a little at a time, that is backpropagation.

questions.prompt: When the vowel network starts training, its accuracy is about twenty percent. Why twenty percent and not zero?
questions.answer: There are five vowels, and at the start the weights are random, so the network is just guessing. Guessing among five choices is right about one time in five, which is twenty percent, so twenty percent is chance, not zero.

questions.prompt: Why does the vowel network level off well below perfect accuracy?
questions.answer: The vowel data overlap a lot, so recordings of different vowels land right on top of each other in F1 and F2. No setting of the weights can separate recordings that sit in the same place, so the network learns something, well above chance, but cannot become perfect.

questions.prompt: Why does real vowel data make AI hard?
questions.answer: If every vowel sat in its own spot in F1 and F2, recognizing vowels would be easy. Instead different people’s vowels overlap a lot, so the network has to see the data many times to find what really separates the vowels, and some recordings can never be separated.

questions.prompt: If the network already gets a training row right, what does it learn from that row? Why can that be a problem?
questions.answer: It learns nothing from that row, because there is no error to learn from. That is a problem because a network can get rows right by accident and stop learning early, without learning the real pattern, the same way children who say "went" correctly at first later say "goed" once they learn the rule.

questions.prompt: What is the learning rate, and what happens to learning when it is high versus low? What does the loss mean?
questions.answer: The loss is the mistake, how far the network’s output is from the desired output. The learning rate sets how big a step the weights take to fix that mistake. A high learning rate learns fast but can be inaccurate and jump around, and a low learning rate learns slowly but carefully and accurately.

questions.prompt: Starting from net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 3), nn.Linear(3, 2), nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.Linear(4, 5)), write the code with an extra hidden layer of three neurons right after the input, and adjust the other layers.
questions.answer: The new code is net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 3), nn.Linear(3, 3), nn.Linear(3, 2), nn.Linear(2, 4), nn.Linear(4, 5)). The first line still takes the two inputs and makes the new layer of three neurons, and the next line takes those three numbers, so every line takes in exactly as many numbers as the line before it makes.

questions.prompt: The network was trained ten times, each time from different random weights. What happened, and what does that tell us?
questions.answer: The runs took different paths, rising and dipping at different times, but they ended in about the same place. So where the weights start changes the path of learning, but with the same data the network ends up learning about as much each time.
rubric: Start changes the route, not the result.

questions.prompt: When the sigmoid is switched on for the hidden neurons, the decision changes completely. Is that learning? Why or why not?
questions.answer: It is not learning, because no weight changed. Only the rule for each neuron’s activation changed, and since later neurons depend on earlier ones, everything downstream was recalculated and the decision moved. Learning only happens when the weights change.

questions.prompt: People say AI has nothing to do with human cognition. Why is that false, according to how neural networks were built?
questions.answer: Neural networks copy discoveries about animal brains. Brains have neurons that collect information from many other neurons, which became the inner product, and Adrian found that neurons are nearly digital, which became the sigmoid. Engineers built in each discovery and then added their own ideas, so a big reason AI works is that it duplicates what animal brains do.

options.feedback: Correct. Chance depends on the number of categories.

options.text: About 0 percent, because the network knows nothing
options.feedback: Guessing is still right sometimes.

options.text: About 50 percent, because every guess is right or wrong
options.feedback: There are four choices, not two.

options.text: About 100 percent, because the formants are clear
options.feedback: Random weights cannot be accurate.

questions.answer: Correct. Chance depends on the number of categories.
rubric: The best answer is About 25 percent, because random guessing is right one time in four.

questions.prompt: What does a single neuron take in and give back? What about a neural network, and a large language model?
questions.answer: A single neuron takes in a list of numbers and gives back one number. A neural network takes in one list of numbers and gives back a whole list of decisions, a probability distribution. A large language model takes in many lists of numbers, one for each moment in a sequence, and gives back one decision about what comes next.
rubric: LLM predicts what comes next from many vectors.

questions.prompt: Describe the Gestalt principle of closure, and how GPT uses it as a principle for learning.
questions.answer: Closure is our ability to fill in what is missing using what we already know, so we see a triangle even when no triangle is drawn. GPT learns the same way. It takes a sequence, treats the next part as missing, and predicts it, and when its guess is wrong its weights are changed, so after an enormous number of completions it knows the language.

questions.prompt: Why is a large language model called a dynamical system?
questions.answer: A dynamical system applies a rule to its current state to get a new state, again and again. A large language model takes the vectors so far and turns them into a prediction of the next one, then that new item is added and the process repeats. That is the same kind of system as masses and springs, which is why the Nobel Prize for AI was in physics.
rubric: Rule applied to the state repeatedly.
Same family as masses and springs.

questions.prompt: What makes Jordan’s network recurrent, and how is it different from a Sequential network?
questions.answer: It is recurrent because it takes its output and sends it back into part of its input, so each step depends on what it did before. A Sequential network just passes information forward through one layer after another, while Jordan’s network had parts working in parallel and fed back over time, which suits movements that unfold in sequence, like speech.

questions.prompt: What is an agentic system, and how did a critic help with hallucination?
questions.answer: An agentic system is a graph of large language models, each with its own job, passing their outputs to one another. One of them can act as a critic that checks another’s answer, and having a critic in the graph is what fixed hallucination, because made-up answers get caught before they come out.

questions.prompt: A large language model takes fifteen vectors and predicts the sixteenth. What can those vectors stand for?
questions.answer: A vector is just a list of numbers, so it can stand for almost anything, such as words, sounds, pixels or molecules. The model only ever sees the vectors, so it plays the same game of predicting the next one with the same architecture, whatever the vectors stand for.
rubric: A vector is a list of numbers.

questions.prompt: Why can a large language model hallucinate?
questions.answer: It predicts the next thing from past data. When something new happens that the past data does not cover, it still makes a prediction, and that prediction can be made up, which is why some systems are now told to say "I don’t know" instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: Why do people’s guesses for the next letter spread out after "ra_" but narrow sharply at the start of a word?
questions.answer: Once a vowel has come, the onset is over and almost any consonant can follow, so after "ra_" many letters are possible and guesses spread out. At the start of a word, the letters have to form an onset that English allows, so the choices narrow to exactly those combinations.
rubric: At the start, only legal onsets.

questions.prompt: What is the core calculation inside a large language model, and where is its knowledge?
questions.answer: The core calculation is the inner product, multiplying numbers by weights and adding them, done billions or trillions of times. The knowledge is in the W’s, the weights, just as in a single network, so whatever the model knows, such as how to write an essay, is stored in those numbers.

options.text: An onset
options.feedback: Correct.

options.feedback: A coda comes after the vowel.

options.text: A formant
options.feedback: A formant is a frequency of the vocal tract.

options.text: A head
options.feedback: A head is part of a language model layer.

questions.answer: An onset
rubric: The best answer is An onset.

questions.prompt: What are heads in a large language model, and how do they relate to layers?
questions.answer: A head is a processing part that helps improve the numerical representation of the sequence, like an expert giving advice on how to improve. Several heads work in parallel inside one layer, and their advice is combined before the vectors move on. The layers come one after another, so each layer takes the improved representation from the one before and improves it further, until the model can predict the next item.
rubric: Many heads in parallel within a layer.

questions.prompt: In a sentence that starts with "the dog," then talks about my parents and people far away, and only then reaches the verb, why is predicting "barks" hard, and what helps?
questions.answer: The verb has to agree with "dog," but "dog" is far back in the sequence, with other singular and plural words in between. So the information needed for the prediction is spread through the sequence. Attention heads consult the whole sequence to work out which relationships matter, so the model can connect the verb to "dog" despite the words about the parents.
rubric: Heads link the verb to dog.

questions.prompt: In an agentic system, when one LLM revises another’s draft, are the models being retrained? Explain.
questions.answer: No. The individual LLMs are already trained, and their weights stay fixed while they exchange drafts and instructions in language. Revising a response changes the answer, while training changes the weights, which only happens when a model learns from its mistakes.

questions.prompt: How is the depth of a large language model like time in a dynamical system such as the oscillator?
questions.answer: A dynamical system starts from initial conditions and applies its rule again and again to get each new state. In a language model, the input vectors are the starting state, and each layer transforms the representations from the layer before, so going deeper through the layers plays the role that going forward in time plays for the oscillator.
rubric: Depth plays the role of time.

questions.prompt: Fifteen vectors can be words, sound frames, picture patches or amino acids. What stays the same and what changes?
questions.answer: The task stays the same, which is to take x1 through x15 and predict x16, and the numerical form of the vectors stays the same. What changes is what the numbers stand for and what order they follow, time for sound frames, a reading order through space for picture patches and positions along a chain for amino acids.

questions.prompt: Why is "Atlantic" a fine English word while "tlantic" is not, even though both contain t and l together?
questions.answer: In At·lan·tic, the t ends one syllable and the l begins the next, so they meet across a syllable boundary. In "tlantic," tl would have to be an onset at the start of a word, and English does not allow tl as an onset. So a syllable boundary changes which sequences are possible.
rubric: t and l across a boundary.
tl is not an English onset.

questions.prompt: A small model was designed to learn English word patterns by guessing the next letter. What was its design, and what came out of the first run?
questions.answer: The model was designed with four attention heads in each of five layers and sixty-four numbers in each token vector, trained on about a thousand words. The first run still produced mostly gibberish, with only a tentative hint of vowels. So guessing the next letter of English is hard even for an LLM, even though people find it easy, and more training and more words were proposed rather than achieved.

questions.prompt: How does a large language model learn from a training sentence?
questions.answer: The training sentence gives both the sequence so far and the actual next word. The model predicts the next word, its prediction is compared with the real one, and when the answer is wrong its weights are changed, so over many sentences its predictions improve.
rubric: Sequence and the true next word.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a multilingual system and a multimodal system?
questions.answer: A multilingual system learns how words go together in more than one language, which is harder when the languages have very different structures. A multimodal system connects different kinds of information, such as text, speech and pictures, and learns how they correspond to each other.
rubric: Multimodal means several kinds of information.
